title: Cap. VI tip: Maresius and others — Rivetus deferred; Scripture arguments next
pass_a_gloss: Chapter Six. That the arguments of the most distinguished D. Maresius prove no other imputation of Adam's first sin than the consequent or mediate. After the last National Synod, for the imputation of Adam's first sin there wrote in printed books (those I have seen) the most distinguished men Andreas Rivetus, Samuel Maresius, Ant. Garissolius, Charles Daubuz, and Stephen Blanc, and many others in manuscript. But the first of them, the most celebrated Rivetus, judged he should fight not by Scripture's authority or by reasons, but by testimonies of learned men scraped together from everywhere — even of men still living, some of whose names had been unheard of by us before; so for now let him be omitted. For those who bring Scripture testimonies and arguments ought to be heard first. We do not ask what men think, but what we ought to think, what God has willed us to think. The rule of our faith is God's word, not men's opinions. These therefore rejected to the last place, let us look at the arguments drawn from the Scriptures.
pass_b_english: Chapter Six. That the arguments of the most distinguished D. Maresius prove no other imputation of Adam’s first sin than the consequent or mediate.

After the last National Synod, several most distinguished men wrote in print — at least among the books I have seen — for the imputation of Adam’s first sin: Andreas Rivetus, Samuel Maresius, Antoine Garissoles, Charles Daubuz, and Stephen Blanc. Many others wrote in manuscript. The first of them, the celebrated Rivetus, chose to fight neither by Scripture’s authority nor by reasons, but by testimonies of learned men scraped together from every quarter, including living writers whose names we had never even heard of before. For now, then, set him aside. Hear first those who bring Scripture’s testimonies and arguments. We are not asking what men think; we are asking what we ought to think, and what God has willed us to think. God’s word is the rule of our faith, not men’s opinions. Push those opinion-collectors to the rear, and let us examine the arguments drawn from the Scriptures.
source_text:
CAPUT VI. Non aliam imputationem primi Adae peccati, quam consequentem seu mediatam, Argumenta Clariss. D. Maresii probare.

Post ultimam Synodum Nationalem pro imputatione primi Adae peccati scripserunt libris typis excusis, quos quidem viderim, Clarissimi viri, Andreas Rivetus, Samuel Maresius, Ant. Garissolius, Carolus Daubuz, et Steph. Blancus, manuscriptis vero alii complures. Sed primus illorum celeberrimus Rivetus non auctoritate Scripturae, nec rationibus, sed corrasis undecunque potuit virorum doctorum testimoniis, etiam adhuc viventium, eorumque nonnullorum, quorum nomen nobis antea inauditum fuerat, pugnandum sibi censuit; itaque nunc quidem omittatur. Docet enim prius audiri eos qui testimonia Scripturae, et argumenta afferunt. Non enim quaerimus quid homines sentiant, sed quid nobis sentiendum sit, quid Deus nos sentire voluerit. Regula fidei nostrae est Dei verbum, non hominum opiniones. His ergo in ultimum locum rejectis, deprompta e Scripturis argumenta inspiciamus.
